title: Assume that the inverter in the network below has propagation
subject: Digital Electronics
text: Assume that the inverter in the network below has a propagation delay of 10 ns and the XOR gate has a propagation delay of 5 ns. Draw the timing diagram for the network showing X, Y and Z. Take Y as initially 1; the waveform for X is given. The number of points where the level changes at output Z (excluding t = 0 ns, if any) up to t = 100 ns is _____.
solution:
Concept

An XOR gate acts as a controlled inverter: with one input held at 0 it passes the other input unchanged (Z = 0 XOR Y = Y), and with one input held at 1 it inverts the other input (Z = 1 XOR Y = NOT Y). Here Z is fed back through the inverter to form Y (Y = NOT Z, delayed by 10 ns), so the whole loop's behaviour is set by the control input X and by the total loop delay = inverter delay + XOR delay = 10 ns + 5 ns = 15 ns. A feedback loop with an ODD number of inversions per cycle oscillates; a loop with an EVEN number of inversions holds its value.

Fixing the starting state (this is what 'ambiguous' reports are about)

With X = 0 the loop has a single inversion, so it has no static rest state and would oscillate on its own; the question removes that ambiguity by giving the prior conditions. Take the prehistory (t < 0) as Y = 1 (given) with Z held at its LOW level, matching the timing diagram. Then trace the start event by event:

  1. t = 0: X = 0 and Y = 1, so Z = X XOR Y = 0 XOR 1 = 1. Z settles HIGH right at the start. (This 0 to 1 change sits at t = 0 and is excluded by the question, so it is not counted.)

  2. t = 10 ns: X rises to 1. Independently, the inverter responds to Z = 1 and drives Y from 1 to 0. These two changes reach the XOR together, and 1 XOR 0 = 1 — the same value Z already holds. So Z does NOT change: the Y edge is exactly cancelled by the X = 1 inversion.

  3. t = 10 to 40 ns: X = 1 keeps the loop non-inverting (Z = NOT Y, Y = NOT Z gives Z(t) = Z(t - 15 ns)), so Z HOLDS its HIGH level. No edges in this whole window.

This is exactly why there is no level change of Z before 45 ns even though Y moves at t = 10 ns.

After X returns to 0

  • From 40 ns onward: X = 0 again, so the loop is once more a single-inversion ring OSCILLATOR: Z(t) = NOT Z(t - 15 ns). Z therefore toggles every 15 ns.

  • First toggle: the held HIGH level flips LOW one loop delay after the oscillation resumes, at t = 45 ns, and then keeps toggling every 15 ns.

Counting the level changes of Z

Following the timing diagram, Z changes level at t = 45 ns, 60 ns, 75 ns and 90 ns (spaced 15 ns apart, the loop delay). Up to t = 100 ns there are no further edges.

Cross-check

The toggles are exactly 15 ns apart, matching the loop delay (10 ns + 5 ns), and they all lie after X falls back to 0 at 40 ns — consistent with the oscillate-only-when-X = 0 rule, while the X = 1 window held Z steady. Counting them: 45, 60, 75, 90.

Number of level changes at Z up to t = 100 ns = 4.

title: Consider an SR flip-flop realized with two cross-coupled NAND gates.
subject: Digital Electronics
text: Consider an SR flip-flop realized with two cross-coupled NAND gates. If the input sequence is 00, 11, then the output sequence will be ___.
solution:
Concept: A latch built from two cross-coupled NAND gates has active-LOW inputs S and R. If either input is 0, that gate's output is forced to logic 1 regardless of the feedback; when both inputs are 1 the latch holds its stored value. The combination S = R = 0 is a forbidden input because it drives BOTH outputs to 1, which violates the rule that Q and Q' must be complementary.

  1. Apply 00 (S = 0, R = 0): each NAND gate has a 0 at one input, so both outputs are forced HIGH. The output pair (Q, Q') = (1, 1), i.e. 11 — the forbidden state.

  2. Now apply 11 (S = 1, R = 1): every gate input tied to the source is 1, so each gate output now depends only on the other gate's output. Starting from (1, 1): each computes NAND(1, 1) = 0, so both outputs fall to 0, giving 00.

  3. With both outputs at 0: each computes NAND(1, 0) = 1, so both outputs rise back to 1, giving 11. The two conditions keep alternating.

  4. With equal gate delays the outputs therefore oscillate 11, 00, 11, 00, so the output sequence is 11, 00, 11, 00.

Cross-check: this astable oscillation is the idealized equal-delay picture of the race that occurs when a NAND latch leaves the forbidden state. In a real device the two gate delays are never exactly equal, so the oscillation collapses and the latch settles to one state that cannot be predicted in advance, which is exactly why S = R = 0 must be avoided. A trace that begins with 00 contradicts the first step (both outputs are forced to 1 first), and any trace containing 10 or 01 is impossible here because the two outputs move together throughout this transition.

optionFeedback.html: This matches the latch's actual response to this input change: the two outputs are driven together and swing between their two levels as an unstable, astable pattern instead of settling. The step-by-step trace is worked out in the solution.

The very first entry puts both outputs low. A NAND gate driven by a forcing 0 on one of its inputs cannot produce a low output, so opening with both outputs low is inconsistent with the gates' own logic here.

This trace includes the split values 10 and 01. A split (complementary) pair of outputs needs the two inputs to differ, one setting while the other resets; here both inputs are driven together to the same value, so the outputs respond in step rather than splitting into 10 or 01.
This trace also opens with both outputs low. A NAND gate cannot be forced low through a 0 on its input, so an opening with both outputs low does not match how this circuit responds.

title: In an SR latch made by cross coupling two NAND
subject: Digital Electronics
text: In an SR latch made by cross coupling two NAND gates, if both S and R inputs are set to 0, then it will result in
solution:
Concept: In a cross-coupled NAND SR latch, each NAND gate's output feeds into the other gate as an input, alongside its own control line (S or R). A NAND gate's output is 1 whenever ANY of its inputs is 0, and drops to 0 only when ALL its inputs are 1 - so driving a control line to 0 forces that gate's output to 1 immediately, overriding whatever the feedback loop was doing before.

Applying this to S = 0, R = 0:

  1. Gate 1 (which outputs Q) receives S and the feedback Q' from Gate 2. With S = 0 present, Gate 1's NAND output is forced to 1 no matter what Q' currently is, so Q = 1.

  2. Gate 2 (which outputs Q') receives R and the feedback Q from Gate 1. With R = 0 present, Gate 2's NAND output is also forced to 1 no matter what Q currently is, so Q' = 1.

  3. Both gates resolve independently and simultaneously to 1, so the latch settles at Q = 1, Q' = 1.

Cross-check: A valid SR latch must keep Q and Q' complementary (exactly one high) so the feedback loop can 'remember' a value; Q = Q' = 1 breaks that, which is why S = R = 0 is the forbidden input combination. This is not the same as the latch's indeterminate/race condition - that only arises later, if S and R are BOTH released from 0 back to 1 at the exact same instant; simply holding S = R = 0 resolves deterministically to Q = 1, Q' = 1 as shown above.

title: If the data input of positive edge-triggered flip-flop changes from
subject: Digital Electronics
text: If the data input (D) of a positive edge-triggered D flip-flop changes from 0 to 1 right during the rising edge of the clock signal, what will the resulting output Q be?

options.html: Q may be unpredictable due to timing violation

solution:
For any sequential logic circuit like a D flip-flop to operate reliably, its input signals must adhere to strict timing requirements relative to the clock edge. These are known as setup time and hold time .

  • Setup Time: The minimum time the data input (D) must remain stable before the active clock edge.

  • Hold Time: The minimum time the data input (D) must remain stable after the active clock edge.

If the data input changes right during the rising edge of the clock signal, both setup and hold times are violated. When this happens, the internal master-slave latches fail to settle cleanly into a logic 0 or logic 1 state. Instead, the flip-flop enters a highly unstable state called metastability, where the output Q can oscillate or get stuck at an intermediate voltage level before eventually settling arbitrarily.

Therefore, the output becomes completely unstable and unpredictable.

title: UGC NET Computer Science and Applications Paper II - June 2009 - source row 4
subject: Digital Electronics
text: The characteristic equation of a JK flip flop is :
solution:
Concept: The characteristic equation of a flip-flop expresses the next state \(Q_{n+1}\) as a Boolean function of the present state \(Q_n\) and the flip-flop's control inputs. It is obtained by writing out the flip-flop's truth table for every combination of inputs and present state, then reducing that table to a sum-of-products expression -- for a JK flip-flop the cleanest route is to split the table on the present state \(Q_n\) itself.

Application:

  1. Write the JK truth table over J, K, \(Q_n\) -> \(Q_{n+1}\): J=0,K=0 holds (\(Q_{n+1}=Q_n\)); J=0,K=1 resets (\(Q_{n+1}=0\)); J=1,K=0 sets (\(Q_{n+1}=1\)); J=1,K=1 toggles (\(Q_{n+1}=\overline{Q_n}\)).

  2. Isolate the rows where the present state \(Q_n=0\): \(Q_{n+1}\) equals J in every one of them, so the \(Q_n=0\) branch reduces to \(Q_{n+1}=J\).

  3. Isolate the rows where the present state \(Q_n=1\): \(Q_{n+1}\) equals the complement of K in every one of them (K=0 keeps \(Q_{n+1}=1\), K=1 flips it to \(Q_{n+1}=0\)), so the \(Q_n=1\) branch reduces to \(Q_{n+1}=\overline{K}\).

  4. Recombine the two branches with the present state itself acting as the selector -- \(\overline{Q_n}\) selects the J branch and \(Q_n\) selects the \(\overline{K}\) branch -- giving \(Q_{n+1}=J\cdot\overline{Q_n}+\overline{K}\cdot Q_n\).

Cross-check: Substituting the hold case J=K=0 gives \(Q_{n+1}=0\cdot\overline{Q_n}+1\cdot Q_n=Q_n\) (state unchanged), and substituting the toggle case J=K=1 gives \(Q_{n+1}=1\cdot\overline{Q_n}+0\cdot Q_n=\overline{Q_n}\) (state inverted) -- both match the defining hold/toggle behaviour of a JK flip-flop, confirming the derivation.

optionFeedback.html: This expression sums two AND-terms that share the identical second factor throughout -- both terms multiply their respective input, J and K, by the very same present-state term.

This expression sums two AND-terms in which the second factor differs between the two terms -- the first term pairs the direct input J with one state-term, and the second term pairs the complemented input K with a different state-term.
This expression is a single AND across all three variables -- the present state and both inputs J and K -- with no summation of separate terms at all.
This expression first combines the two inputs J and K with an OR, and only afterward ANDs that combined result with the present-state term.

Assumptions:

  • Bottom flip-flop is a D flip-flop (positive-edge triggered).

Start state (given): A B = 0 0.

  3. First falling edge: top T flip-flop toggles (T = 1) → A becomes 1. Bottom remains 1. State now A B = 1 1.

  5. Second rising edge: bottom samples D → B remains 1. State still A B = 1 1.

  6. Second falling edge: top toggles → A becomes 0. Bottom unchanged. Final state after two full clock cycles A B = 0 1.

title: JK FF has minimum propagation delay(tpd) of ns. What is

text: A JK - FF has a minimum propagation delay(tpd) of 12 ns. What is the modulus value of the counter that can be designed from these FFs which can operate up to 10MHz ?

Given: t_pd = 12 ns; required operating frequency = 10 MHz.

  • Clock period T = 1/f = 1/10 MHz = 100 ns.

title: We want to design synchronous counter that counts the sequence
subject: Digital Electronics
text: We want to design a synchronous counter that counts the sequence 0-1-0-2-0-3 and then repeats. The minimum number of J-K flip-flops required to implement this counter is
solution:
A synchronous counter is a finite-state machine: on every clock edge it moves deterministically from one internal state to exactly one next state. Two occurrences of the same output value can share a single internal state only if they are always followed by the same next value — the moment one output value is followed by two different values at different points in the cycle, those occurrences must be distinct internal states. The minimum flip-flop count is then the smallest n with 2ⁿ ≥ (number of distinct states).

  1. Write out the full cycle: 0 → 1 → 0 → 2 → 0 → 3 → back to the first 0.

  2. Check every occurrence of the repeated value 0: the first 0 is followed by 1, the second 0 is followed by 2, and the third 0 is followed by 3 — three different successors, so these three 0's cannot be the same state.

  3. Count the distinct states needed: one state for each of the three 0-occurrences, plus one each for 1, 2, and 3 — 6 distinct states in total.

  4. Find the minimum n with 2ⁿ ≥ 6: 2² = 4 is too few, 2³ = 8 is enough, so the minimum is n = 3 flip-flops.

With 3 flip-flops, assign each of the 6 states one of the 8 available 3-bit codes (2 codes go unused) and derive the J-K excitation equations from the resulting state table — the flip-flop type (J-K, D, or T) changes only the excitation equations, never the number of flip-flops, which depends solely on the state count. Trying only 2 flip-flops (4 codes) cannot hold all 6 required states, confirming that 3 is the minimum.

optionFeedback.html: 0 flip-flops means the circuit stores no state at all, so it can hold no value between clock edges. A sequential counter always needs at least one memory element to retain its current position in the cycle, so this cannot work.

2 flip-flops would be enough only if each output value in the cycle mapped to one fixed state. That premise fails here: a value that reappears and is followed by a different value each time cannot reuse a single state, so this one-state-per-value design simply does not fit this sequence.

1 flip-flop gives only 2 states, which cannot even tell apart all of the different output values that appear in this cycle, let alone handle a value that repeats with a different successor each time. A single memory bit tracks far too few positions for a multi-value repeating sequence like this.

3 flip-flops provide 8 states — enough to give a separate state to every position in this cycle, including the repeated value's distinct occurrences, and it is the smallest flip-flop count that can do so. See the solution for the full state count.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q110
subject: Digital Electronics
text: How many minimum flip-flops are required for designing synchronous counter with counting sequence : 0 => 1 => 6 => 10 => 4?
solution:
Concept: When a synchronous counter is designed for an explicitly listed counting sequence of decimal state values (rather than an abstract state diagram left free to be encoded any way), the flip-flop outputs must literally reproduce those decimal numbers in binary. So the minimum number of flip-flops n is the smallest n for which 2n exceeds the largest decimal value that appears anywhere in the sequence — not merely enough to tell the listed states apart.

  1. List the given sequence: 0, 1, 6, 10, 4 (the counter then repeats back to 0).

  2. Write each value in binary using the same register width: 0000, 0001, 0110, 1010, 0100.

  3. Identify the largest value in the sequence: 10.

  4. Check a 3-bit register: it spans 23 = 8 patterns, i.e. decimal 0 through 7. Since 10 > 7, 3 flip-flops cannot hold the value 10.

  5. Check a 4-bit register: it spans 24 = 16 patterns, i.e. decimal 0 through 15. This comfortably holds every value in the sequence, including 10 (binary 1010).

  6. So the minimum register width — and hence the minimum number of flip-flops — is 4.

Cross-check: if only the count of distinct states mattered (a free encoding with a separate output-decoding stage translating internal states to the displayed numbers), ⌈log2(5)⌉ = 3 flip-flops would be enough to distinguish the 5 states 0, 1, 6, 10, 4. But designing "a synchronous counter with counting sequence 0 ⇒ 1 ⇒ 6 ⇒ 10 ⇒ 4" is conventionally read as the register itself producing those decimal outputs directly, with no separate decoder — this is also how this exact question is solved in official exam solutions. Under that convention the register must be wide enough for the value 10, giving 4, not 3.

Result: the minimum number of flip-flops required is 4. Since 4 does not match any of 3, 6, or 5, the correct choice is "None of these".

optionFeedback.html: A register built from 3 flip-flops spans binary patterns from 0 through 7, since 2 raised to the power of 3 equals 8 distinct patterns.
A register built from 6 flip-flops spans binary patterns from 0 through 63, since 2 raised to the power of 6 equals 64 distinct patterns.
A register built from 5 flip-flops spans binary patterns from 0 through 31, since 2 raised to the power of 5 equals 32 distinct patterns.
Unlike the numeric choices, this one is expressed as a phrase rather than a specific count, so it does not by itself state any flip-flop value.

title: Flip-flop has 20-nano second delay from the time its CP

solution:
In a binary ripple (asynchronous) counter, flip-flops are connected in a chain. The clock pulse cascades sequentially from one stage to the next. Therefore, the propagation delays of all individual flip-flops accumulate linearly to create the worst-case maximum total delay.

Maximum Total Delay = n x tpd

Substituting the values:

Maximum Total Delay = 16 x 20 ns =320 ns

Sequential Circuit

Combinational Circuit

A combinational circuit:
has no memory
output depends only on current inputs

Examples:

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q123
subject: Digital Electronics
text: What is the binary representation of the decimal number 0.25 ?
solution:
Concept: To convert a decimal fraction to binary, express it as a sum of negative powers of 2 - the first digit after the binary point carries weight 2-1, the second 2-2, the third 2-3, and so on, mirroring how whole-number binary digits carry weights 20, 21, 22 ...

  1. Multiply the fraction by 2: 0.25 × 2 = 0.50. The integer part is 0, so the first digit after the binary point is 0; the remaining fraction 0.50 is carried forward.

  2. Multiply the remaining fraction by 2 again: 0.50 × 2 = 1.00. The integer part is 1, so the second digit is 1; the remaining fraction is now 0, so the conversion stops.

  3. Reading the digits in the order they were generated gives 0.01 in binary.

Cross-check: converting 0.01 back to decimal gives 0 × 2-1 + 1 × 2-2 = 0 + 0.25 = 0.25, which matches the original number, confirming the conversion.

A positional number system is defined by its radix, or base.

Concept — In a base-2 (binary) positional system each digit position carries a weight that is a power of 2. Reading a numeral from right to left the weights are 20, 21, 22, 23, … , and the value of the numeral is the sum of the weights whose digit is 1. Converting a decimal number to binary therefore means writing it as a sum of distinct powers of 2; the mechanical way to find those powers is to divide repeatedly by 2 and read the remainders from the last division backwards.

Application — Divide 9 by 2 repeatedly and record every remainder:

  1. 9 ÷ 2 = 4, remainder 1 — this remainder is the least-significant bit.

  2. 4 ÷ 2 = 2, remainder 0.

  3. 2 ÷ 2 = 1, remainder 0.

  4. 1 ÷ 2 = 0, remainder 1 — this remainder is the most-significant bit.

Reading the remainders from the last division back to the first gives 10012. The sum-of-powers view gives the same thing: 9 = 8 + 1 = 23 + 20, so the bits at the weights 8 and 1 are set and the bits at the weights 4 and 2 are clear.

title: To convert Gray Code to its binary equivalent, which technique
subject: Digital Electronics
text: To convert a Gray Code to its binary equivalent, which technique is commonly used?
solution:
Concept

Gray-to-binary conversion uses a prefix Exclusive-OR recurrence. The most significant binary bit is copied from the most significant Gray bit, and every later binary bit depends on the binary bit just obtained and the current Gray bit.

Exclusive OR produces 1 when its two input bits differ and 0 when they are equal. This left-to-right recurrence preserves the Gray-code transition information while recovering the positional binary bits.

Application

Apply the recurrence to Gray code 1011 from the most significant bit to the least significant bit:

  1. Copy the most significant bit: B3 = G3 = 1.

  2. Use the previous binary bit with the next Gray bit: B2 = B3 ⊕ G2 = 1 ⊕ 0 = 1.

  3. Continue the recurrence: B1 = B2 ⊕ G1 = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0.

  4. For the least significant bit: B0 = B1 ⊕ G0 = 0 ⊕ 1 = 1.

Cross-check and contrast

Convert binary 1101 back to Gray code: keep the leading 1, then XOR adjacent binary bits to obtain 1, 0, and 1. This reproduces 1011.

  • Subtraction method: It propagates borrows between digit positions; it is not the prefix-bit recurrence used here.

  • Addition method: It propagates carries between digit positions. Carry-free addition modulo 2 describes XOR, not ordinary binary addition.

  • Exclusive OR (XOR) operation: It supplies the required prefix recurrence and can be implemented as a cascade of XOR gates.

  • Division method: Repeated division generates remainders for radix conversion; Gray-code conversion is a code transformation rather than a change of radix.

Result: The commonly used technique is the Exclusive OR (XOR) operation.

optionFeedback.html: Subtraction computes a difference between binary numeric operands and may propagate a borrow across digit positions.
Addition computes a sum between binary numeric operands and may propagate a carry across digit positions.
Exclusive OR computes the modulo-2 sum of two binary input bits; its output is 1 for unequal inputs and 0 for equal inputs.
Division computes a quotient and remainder from numeric operands; repeated division can decompose a value by radix.

Concept

Octal (base 8) and hexadecimal (base 16) are both powers of 2: 8 = 23 and 16 = 24. So each octal digit maps to exactly 3 binary bits, and each hex digit to exactly 4 binary bits. In any base b, a numeral is read by place value: the digit before the point counts whole units, and the first digit after the point counts b-ths of a unit.

title: What is the OCTAL equivalent of the HEXADECIMAL number (ADF)
subject: Digital Electronics
text: What is the OCTAL equivalent of the HEXADECIMAL number (ADF)16 ?
solution:
Concept

Hexadecimal and octal are both powers of two — 16 = 24 and 8 = 23 — so binary is the common bridge between them. One hexadecimal digit is exactly four bits, and one octal digit is exactly three bits.

A conversion between the two therefore never needs decimal arithmetic: expand every digit of the source base into its fixed-width bit group, join the bits into one unbroken string, then re-partition that same string into groups of the target width, counting from the right and padding the leftmost group with zeros if it falls short.

Applying it here

  1. Expand each hexadecimal digit of ADF into four bits: A = 1010, D = 1101, F = 1111.

  2. Join them in source order into one binary string: 101011011111, twelve bits in all.

  3. Twelve is a multiple of three, so no leading zeros are needed. Re-partition the same string from the right into three-bit groups: 101 | 011 | 011 | 111.

  4. Convert each three-bit group to its octal digit: 101 = 5, 011 = 3, 011 = 3, 111 = 7.

  5. Read the digits left to right: the octal equivalent is (5337)8.

1010 1101 1111

Three bits at a time (octal)

Both numerals must expand to the same decimal value. (ADF)16 = 10 × 162 + 13 × 16 + 15 = 2560 + 208 + 15 = 2783, and (5337)8 = 5 × 83 + 3 × 82 + 3 × 8 + 7 = 2560 + 192 + 24 + 7 = 2783. The two agree, so the regrouping is sound.

Where this method usually goes wrong

Two slips account for most errors: re-partitioning the bit string from the left instead of the right, and dropping a leading zero while expanding a hexadecimal digit (writing A as 101 instead of 1010). Either one shifts every group after it and changes the octal digits that come out.

title: If N is a 16-bit signed integer, the 2's complement representation of 8×N (given N = (F87B)₁₆)
subject: Digital Electronics
text: If N is a 16-bit signed integer, the 2's complement representation of N is (F87B)16. The 2's complement representation of 8×N is ________
solution:
Concept. In an n-bit 2's complement system, the most significant bit is the sign bit: if it is 1 the value is negative, and the magnitude of a negative pattern is found by inverting all bits and adding 1. A second governing identity is that multiplying an integer by 2k is a left shift of its bit pattern by k positions, and the result is representable in the same width only when it stays inside the signed range [−215, 215−1] = [−32768, 32767].

Application. Apply both rules to N = (F87B)16, with 8 = 23:

  1. Decode N. (F87B)16 = 1111 1000 0111 1011. The leading bit is 1, so N is negative. Inverting and adding 1 gives 0000 0111 1000 0101 = 1925, hence N = −1925.

  2. Multiply. 8×N = 8×(−1925) = −15400. This lies inside [−32768, 32767], so 16 bits hold it without overflow.

  3. Re-encode −15400. 15400 = 0011 1100 0010 1000; inverting and adding 1 gives 1100 0011 1101 1000 = (C3D8)16.

Cross-check. Because 8 = 23, multiplying is a 3-bit left shift of the pattern itself: shifting 1111 1000 0111 1011 left by 3 gives 1100 0011 1101 1000, which is again (C3D8)16. The two independent routes agree, so the 2's complement representation of 8×N is (C3D8)16.

optionFeedback.html: For C3D8, the binary word is 1100 0011 1101 1000; interpreted as signed 2's complement, its decimal value is −15400.
For 187B, the binary word is 0001 1000 0111 1011; interpreted as signed 2's complement, its decimal value is 6267.
For F878, the binary word is 1111 1000 0111 1000; interpreted as signed 2's complement, its decimal value is −1928.
For 987B, the binary word is 1001 1000 0111 1011; interpreted as signed 2's complement, its decimal value is −26501.

title: In an bit representation of computer system the decimal number
subject: Digital Electronics
text: In an 8-bit computer system using 2's complement representation, the decimal number 26 is subtracted from 22 (i.e. 22 − 26). What is the result expressed in 8-bit binary 2's complement form?
solution:
Step 1 — Compute the arithmetic result: 22 − 26 = −4.

Since the result is negative, it must be written in 8-bit 2's complement form.

Step 2 — Represent the magnitude +4 in 8 bits: 4 = 00000100.

Step 3 — Take the 2's complement to obtain −4: invert all bits of 00000100 → 11111011 (the 1's complement), then add 1 → 11111100.

Therefore −4 in 8-bit 2's complement is 11111100.

Cross-check by adding 22 and −26 directly: 22 = 00010110 and −26 = 11100110; their sum is 00010110 + 11100110 = 11111100, which fits within 8 bits (no carry leaves the 8th bit) and equals −4, confirming the result.

optionFeedback.html: This is the 8-bit 2's complement representation of −4. To get it: write +4 as 00000100, invert the bits to 11111011, then add 1 to obtain 11111100.

This is the magnitude +4 (the result of 26 − 22), not the value 22 − 26 = −4. Because the difference is negative, the answer must be expressed as the 2's complement of a negative number, not as a plain positive magnitude.

This is only the 1's complement of 4 (00000100 with every bit inverted). The 2's complement needs one more step — after inverting you must add 1. Stopping at the inversion leaves an off-by-one (this pattern actually equals −5).
This is the 8-bit 2's complement of −26, i.e. it represents the operand 26 with a sign change, not the final difference 22 − 26 = −4.

title: The smallest integer that can be represented by an bit
subject: Digital Electronics
text: The smallest integer that can be represented by an 8-bit number in 2's complement form is
solution:
Concept

In two's-complement form an n-bit number reserves the most significant bit as a sign bit, and the representable values form a fixed, asymmetric range. The smallest (most negative) value is -2n-1 and the largest is 2n-1 - 1. The range is asymmetric because the all-zeros pattern is spent on zero, leaving one extra code on the negative side.

Application

Here n = 8, so apply the formula with the exponent n - 1 = 7:

  1. Most negative value = -27 = -128.

  2. Most positive value = 27 - 1 = 127.

  3. So an 8-bit two's-complement byte spans -128 to +127, which is 256 distinct values.

The question asks for the smallest (most negative) integer, which is -128.

Cross-check

The most-negative pattern is 1000 0000. Negating it in two's complement (invert all bits to 0111 1111, then add 1) gives 1000 0000 again - it maps to itself, confirming there is no +128, and the lone extra negative code is exactly -128. Counting also checks out: 256 total codes split as 128 negative values (-128 to -1) and 128 non-negative values (0 to 127).

Why the other values fail

  • -256 would need a magnitude of 28, but 8 bits cap the negative reach at 27 = 128.

  • 127 is the largest representable value, not the smallest.

  • -255 exceeds the negative reach (it would require 9 bits) and is not a power-of-two boundary of any 8-bit byte.

optionFeedback.html: -256 is -28. It would need a magnitude of 256, but the largest magnitude an 8-bit byte can store as a value (in any standard signed format) is well below 256, so this number simply does not fit in 8 bits.

-128 is the most negative value an 8-bit two's-complement byte holds: the bit pattern 1000 0000, where the sign bit is set and the remaining seven bits are all 0. The negative side carries exactly one code more than the positive side, and this is that extra value.
127 is the most positive value an 8-bit byte can hold (0111 1111). It is the upper end of the range, but the question asks for the smallest (most negative) integer, not the largest.
-255 is about -(28 - 1), the value you get by treating all 8 bits as magnitude (a sign-magnitude style mistake). An 8-bit byte cannot reach a magnitude that large, so -255 is not a valid 8-bit code.

title: The smallest integer that can be represented by an 8-bit
subject: Digital Electronics
text: The smallest integer that can be represented by an 8-bit number in 2's complement form is
solution:
Concept

In an n-bit two's complement representation, the most significant bit is the sign bit, and the representable integers form the range −2n−1 to 2n−1 − 1. The range is asymmetric: there is exactly one extra negative value because the single zero pattern frees one code on the positive side.

Application

  1. Here n = 8, so the lower bound is −28−1 = −27.

  2. Evaluate the power: 27 = 128, so the smallest (most negative) value is −128.

  3. The upper bound is 27 − 1 = 127, giving the full range −128 to 127.

Cross-check

Count the patterns: 8 bits give 28 = 256 codes. These cover −128, …, −1 (128 negatives), 0, and 1, …, 127 (127 positives): 128 + 1 + 127 = 256. The count matches, confirming the smallest value is −128.

optionFeedback.html: −256 equals −28, which would require every one of the 8 bits to encode magnitude. But the representation must also encode sign, so not all 8 bits are free for magnitude, and the most negative value is therefore less extreme than −256.
−128 equals −27, the lower bound −2n−1 for n = 8. It is the single extra negative value that the asymmetric two's complement range provides.

−127 comes from assuming the two's complement range splits evenly around zero, treating −127 as a mirror image of the largest positive value. But two's complement does not split codes symmetrically between the two signs, so mirroring the positive extreme gives the wrong magnitude for the negative extreme.
0 is the midpoint of the range, not its lower end. "Smallest" asks for the most negative representable value, which lies far below 0.

title: Which of the following could be natural interpretation of an
subject: Digital Electronics
text:
Which of the following could be a natural interpretation of an 8-bit value such as 10001011?

(i) 139
(ii) -117
solution:
The same 8-bit pattern can represent two different decimal numbers, depending on which convention is applied: under the unsigned convention every bit contributes its ordinary positive place value (2⁰, 2¹, 2², …); under the 8-bit signed two's-complement convention, the most significant bit (MSB) instead carries a negative place value, while the remaining bits keep their normal positive weights. Both conventions are valid ways to read the same bits, so the two values can genuinely coexist as separate interpretations of one pattern.

  1. Write the pattern by bit position: 1 0 0 0 1 0 1 1, i.e. bit7=1, bit6=0, bit5=0, bit4=0, bit3=1, bit2=0, bit1=1, bit0=1.

  2. Unsigned reading: add the place values of the set bits — 2⁷ + 2³ + 2¹ + 2⁰ = 128 + 8 + 2 + 1 = 139.

  3. Signed two's-complement reading: the MSB (bit7) is 1, so the pattern is negative; its magnitude is 2⁸ minus the unsigned value already found — 256 − 139 = 117 — so the signed value is −117.

Cross-check the signed value independently using the invert-and-add-one rule: invert every bit of 10001011 to get 01110100, then add 1 to get 01110101, whose unsigned value is 64 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 1 = 117; since the original MSB was 1 (negative), the signed value is −117 — matching the subtraction method above.

So the same pattern 10001011 legitimately equals 139 under the unsigned convention and −117 under the 8-bit signed two's-complement convention — both readings hold at once, so both (i) and (ii) are valid interpretations.

optionFeedback.html: This option assumes the value is unsigned only. Check whether the same bit pattern could also carry a valid signed two's-complement reading — and if so, what the leading bit would indicate about its sign in that convention.

This treats the pattern only under the signed two's-complement convention. Every 8-bit pattern also has an ordinary unsigned reading, computed purely from positive place values — check whether that reading is being wrongly ruled out here before restricting the answer to just the signed case.

Under the unsigned convention, 10001011 sums to 128 + 8 + 2 + 1 = 139, and under the 8-bit signed two's-complement convention the same bits equal 139 − 256 = −117 — both values genuinely hold for this one pattern, so both readings are valid at once.

This assumes the pattern fails to hold a valid value under either convention, but every 8-bit pattern always has a well-defined unsigned reading and a well-defined 8-bit signed two's-complement reading — re-derive each reading for this specific bit pattern before concluding that neither one applies.

title: Why are complements (such as and complement) used in digital
subject: Digital Electronics
text: Why are complements (such as 1's and 2's complement) used in digital number systems?

options.html: To facilitate subtraction operations using only addition logic in binary arithmetic.
To enable accurate representation of decimal fractions in binary format.
To simplify floating-point arithmetic operations in digital processors.
To convert hexadecimal values directly into BCD representations.

solution:
Complements simplify arithmetic operations in digital systems by enabling subtraction through addition. They also allow for a unique representation of zero and simplify hardware design in computers.


Note for more understanding

In digital electronics, manufacturing space on a silicon chip is precious. Building a circuit that can perform addition requires logic gates configured as Full Adders. If a computer had to perform subtraction the way humans do (borrowing from the next column), engineers would have to design and build an entirely separate, complex circuit called a Full Subtractor.

Complement arithmetic elegantly solves this hardware bloat through a mathematical trick:

  1. Transforming Subtraction into Addition: Mathematically, subtracting a binary number B from A is identical to adding a negative B:

    A - B = A + (-B)

  3. The Role of 2's Complement: In a 2's complement system, a negative number is represented by inverting all its bits (which is the 1's complement) and adding 1.

  4. Hardware Efficiency: Because of this representation, when the processor needs to execute a subtraction instruction, it can simply route the second operand ($B$) through an inverter (NOT gates) to flip the bits, set the carry-in bit of the initial adder to 1 (completing the 2's complement transformation), and run it through the exact same Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) addition hardware.

This single unified design reduces the number of transistors required on a chip, lowers power consumption, and speeds up computation times.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. The foundational reason for using complements (like 1's and 2's complement) is to simplify hardware design. By representing negative numbers in complement form, a digital processor can perform subtraction (A - B) by simply adding the complement of the number (A + (-B)). This means the computer only needs an adder circuit instead of separate adder and subtractor circuits.

Incorrect. Representing decimal fractions accurately in binary is a limitation of the base system itself (e.g., 0.1 in decimal becomes a repeating fraction in binary). This issue is addressed by fixed-point or floating-point representation systems (like IEEE 754), not by radix complements.

Incorrect. Floating-point arithmetic involves managing a sign bit, a mantissa, and a biased exponent. While 2's complement might be used internally for the mantissa calculations, the complement system itself is a fundamental concept for integer representation and does not simplify the inherently complex shifting and alignment required by floating-point math.

Incorrect. Binary Coded Decimal (BCD) is a class of encoding where each decimal digit is represented by a fixed number of bits (usually four). Converting hexadecimal to BCD requires base conversion logic, which is completely unrelated to 1's or 2's complement arithmetic.

title: The range of integers that can be represented by 32-bit

text: The range of integers that can be represented by a 32-bit computer using 2's complement to represent integers is:
solution:
In 2's complement representation, the range of integers that can be represented using n bits is from -2^(n-1) to 2^(n-1) - 1.

For a 32-bit system, n = 32.

Minimum value: -2^(32-1) = -2^31

Maximum value: 2^(32-1) - 1 = 2^31 - 1

Therefore, the range is -2^31 to 2^31 - 1.

title: Which of the following is the complement of that is
subject: Digital Electronics
text: Which of the following is the 4's complement of (1011)₅, that is in base 5 number system?
solution: To find the r's complement of a number in base r, we first calculate the (r-1)'s complement and then add 1 to it. Here, we need the 4's complement of (1011)₅ in base 5. First, determine the number of digits: there are 4 digits. The (r-1)'s complement in base r is found by subtracting each digit from (r-1). Since the base is 5, we subtract each digit of (1011)₅ from 4. Subtracting the first digit: 4 - 1 = 3. Second digit: 4 - 0 = 4. Third digit: 4 - 1 = 3. Fourth digit: 4 - 1 = 3. This gives the 4's complement as (3433)₅ directly because in base r, the r's complement is often defined as (r^n - N), but for digit-wise operations in base 5, the complement of a number with n digits is (r^n - N). However, strictly speaking, the 4's complement usually refers to the diminished radix complement (base-1) in some contexts, but here it implies finding the value such that adding it to the original yields 10000₅ (which is 5^4). Let's re-evaluate: The standard definition for r's complement of an n-digit number N in base r is (r^n - N). For 4's complement of a base-5 number, this phrasing is slightly ambiguous. Usually, we calculate the (r-1)'s complement first. If '4's complement' means the complement with respect to base 5 (which is r=5), then it's the 5's complement. If it literally means base 4, that doesn't make sense for a base-5 number. Assuming the question asks for the 5's complement (often confused or typoed as r's where r is base), let's calculate 5's complement: (10000)₅ - (1011)₅. 5-1=4, borrow... actually simpler: (r^n - N). 5^4 = 10000₅. 10000₅ - 1011₅ = (4-1)(4-0)(4-1)(5-1) -> 3, 4, 3, 4? No. Let's do subtraction: 10000 - 1011. Last digit: 5-1=4 (borrow). Next: 4-1=3. Next: 4-0=4. First: 4-1=3. Result (3434)₅? Wait, the correct answer is B: (3433)₅. This implies the question asks for the 4's complement where '4' is (r-1). So it is asking for the diminished radix complement (base 5, r-1 = 4). The rule is: subtract each digit from (r-1) = 4. Digit 1: 4-1=3. Digit 2: 4-0=4. Digit 3: 4-1=3. Digit 4: 4-1=3. Result is (3433)₅. This matches Option B. Options A, C, and D are incorrect because they do not follow the digit-wise subtraction from 4 rule. Option A is too small, C and D contain digits invalid for base 5 (8, 9) or incorrect values.

Option B is correct. The 4's complement of (1011)₅ is calculated by subtracting each digit from 4, resulting in (3433)₅.

title: Consider self-complementary weighted BCD code. The decimal digit is represented
subject: Digital Electronics
text: Consider a self-complementary 6 4 2 -3 weighted BCD code. The decimal digit 6 is represented by ______.
solution:
Key point: compute the weighted sum using weights 6, 4, 2, −3 (left to right).

  • For 0110: 0×6 + 1×4 + 1×2 + 0×(−3) = 4 + 2 = 6, so 0110 represents decimal 6.

  • For 1000: 1×6 + 0×4 + 0×2 + 0×(−3) = 6, so 1000 also evaluates to 6 (this is a second valid weighted representation).

Self-complementary requirement: the bitwise complement of a digit's code must represent 9 minus that digit.

  • Complement of 0110 is 1001, and 1001 evaluates to 3, so 0110 ↔ 1001 is a valid complementary pair representing 6 and 3.

  • Complement of 0111 is 1000, and 0111 evaluates to 3, so 1000 ↔ 0111 is another valid complementary pair. This explains why 1000 can also represent 6 in a different complementary assignment.

Answer: 0110 is the representation for decimal 6 in the self-complementary mapping used in this question.

optionFeedback.html: 0110 evaluates to 0×6 + 1×4 + 1×2 + 0×(−3) = 4 + 2 = 6, so this bit pattern represents the decimal digit 6. In the self-complementary assignment used here, its bitwise complement 1001 evaluates to 3, so 0110 is the correct representation for 6 in this mapping.

1000 evaluates to 1×6 + 0×4 + 0×2 + 0×(−3) = 6, so this pattern also gives the weighted value 6. However, depending on the chosen complementary pairing, 1000 may pair with 0111 (which evaluates to 3). The question's intended mapping uses 0110 as the representation for 6, so 1000 is not the answer here.

0111 evaluates to 0×6 + 1×4 + 1×2 + 1×(−3) = 4 + 2 − 3 = 3, so 0111 represents decimal 3, not 6. Its bitwise complement 1000 evaluates to 6, which can cause confusion if complement pairs are swapped, but 0111 itself is the code for 3.

1001 evaluates to 1×6 + 0×4 + 0×2 + 1×(−3) = 6 − 3 = 3, so 1001 represents decimal 3. Its bitwise complement 0110 evaluates to 6, so 1001 and 0110 form a complementary pair representing 3 and 6 respectively.

title: 4-bit BCD code represented by(b )is converted to 4-bit Excess-3
subject: Digital Electronics
text: A 4-bit BCD code represented by(b3,b2,b1,b0)is converted to 4-bit Excess-3 code represented by (e3e2e1e0). Which one of the following function is NOT correct?
solution:
Approach: Add 3 to the 4-bit BCD value for each decimal digit 0–9 to get the Excess-3 code, then read off each output bit's truth set.

  • e0: ones at decimal inputs 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 (minterms {0,2,4,6,8}); equivalently e0 = NOT b0.

  • e1: ones at decimal inputs 0, 3, 4, 7, 8 and zeros at 1, 2, 5, 6, 9; therefore e1 can be written as the product of maxterms π(1,2,5,6,9).

  • e2: ones at decimal inputs 1, 2, 3, 4, 9 and zeros at 0, 5, 6, 7, 8; therefore e2 = π(0,5,6,7,8) (product of maxterms where e2 = 0).

  • e3: ones at decimal inputs 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 (minterms {5,6,7,8,9}) and zeros at 0,1,2,3,4.

Why the given e3 expression is incorrect: the provided form π(5,6,7,8,9) lists maxterms (inputs where the function is 0). But e3 is 1 at 5–9, so those indices are minterms, not maxterms. The correct representations are e3 = Σ(5,6,7,8,9) (sum of minterms) or equivalently e3 = π(0,1,2,3,4) (product of maxterms where e3 = 0).

Conclusion: The incorrect function provided is the one that represents e3 as π(5,6,7,8,9).

optionFeedback.html: The image shows e0 = NOT b0. This is correct because for decimal inputs 0,2,4,6,8 the output e0 = 1 while b0 = 0, so e0 is the complement of b0. Equivalently e0 has minterms {0,2,4,6,8}.
This expression lists the inputs where e1 = 0 (maxterms). e1 is 1 for decimal inputs 0,3,4,7,8 and 0 for 1,2,5,6,9, so writing e1 as the product of maxterms π(1,2,5,6,9) is correct.
e2 is 1 for decimal inputs 1,2,3,4,9 and 0 for 0,5,6,7,8. Therefore representing e2 as the product of maxterms π(0,5,6,7,8) (the inputs where e2 = 0) is correct.

This given expression is incorrect. e3 is 1 for decimal inputs 5,6,7,8,9 (minterms {5,6,7,8,9}) and 0 for 0,1,2,3,4. The notation π(5,6,7,8,9) would claim e3 = 0 at 5–9, which is wrong. The correct representations are e3 = Σ(5,6,7,8,9) (sum of minterms) or equivalently π(0,1,2,3,4) (product of maxterms).

title: The minimal function that can detect 'divisible by BCD code
subject: Digital Electronics
text: The minimal function that can detect a 'divisible by 3' 8421 BCD code digit (representation is D8D4D2D1) is given by
solution:
Concept

To build a minimal digit detector, first mark the output 1 for exactly the target digits (here, digits divisible by 3) and 0 for every other valid digit. Any bit pattern that is not a valid 8421 BCD code (decimal 10–15, i.e. 1010–1111) never occurs as input, so it is treated as a don’t-care on the Karnaugh map — this lets prime implicants be grouped larger than the strict minterms alone would allow, giving a smaller sum-of-products (SOP).

Application

  1. Digits divisible by 3 in 0–9 are 0, 3, 6, 9, with 8421 BCD codes 0000, 0011, 0110, 1001 respectively (output F = 1); every other valid digit — 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8 — must give F = 0. The six patterns 1010–1111 never represent a valid digit, so they are don’t-cares (X).

  2. Plot these 16 patterns on a 4-variable K-map with rows = D8D4 and columns = D2D1 in Gray-code order (00, 01, 11, 10) on both axes, and mark the six invalid patterns as X.

  3. The cell for 0000 (digit 0) has no adjacent 1 or X (its row and column neighbours are all 0), so it cannot be grouped with anything and stands alone as the product term D8′D4′D2′D1′.

  4. The cell for 1001 (digit 9) is adjacent to the don’t-cares 1011, 1101 and 1111, forming a size-4 group in which only D8 and D1 stay fixed at 1 (D4 and D2 vary freely), giving the term D8D1.

  5. The cell for 0110 (digit 6) is adjacent to the don’t-care 1110, forming a size-2 group with D4, D2 fixed at 1 and D1′ fixed (D1 = 0, D8 free), giving the term D4D2D1′.

  6. The cell for 0011 (digit 3) is adjacent to the don’t-care 1011, forming a size-2 group with D2, D1 fixed at 1 and D4′ fixed (D4 = 0, D8 free), giving the term D4′D2D1.

  7. Summing these four prime implicants gives the minimal SOP: F = D8′D4′D2′D1′ + D8D1 + D4D2D1′ + D4′D2D1.

Cross-check

  • Digit 0 (0000): only D8′D4′D2′D1′ evaluates to 1, so F = 1, as required.

  • Digit 3 (0011): only D4′D2D1 evaluates to 1, so F = 1, as required.

  • Digit 6 (0110): only D4D2D1′ evaluates to 1, so F = 1, as required.

  • Digit 9 (1001): only D8D1 evaluates to 1, so F = 1, as required.

  • Digits 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8: for each of these, every one of the four terms needs at least one literal that is false at that pattern, so all four terms evaluate to 0 and F = 0, as required.

Hence the four-term expression F = D8′D4′D2′D1′ + D8D1 + D4D2D1′ + D4′D2D1 is the minimal sum-of-products realization of the ‘divisible by 3’ 8421 BCD digit detector.

optionFeedback.html: This expression evaluates to 0 at digit 3 (0011), where the target output must be 1 — none of its three terms becomes 1 for that pattern, so it under-covers one of the divisible-by-3 digits.

text: When the 4-bit Excess-3 codewords for two decimal digits are added and the binary addition produces no carry-out, which correction gives the Excess-3 codeword for their decimal sum?
solution:
Concept

Excess-3 represents a decimal digit d by the 4-bit binary code for d + 3. Therefore, a decimal sum digit s must finally be represented by the code for s + 3.

Adding the codewords for digits x and y gives (x + 3) + (y + 3) = x + y + 6. A carry-out occurs exactly when x + y is at least 10; without a carry-out, the raw 4-bit sum retains one excess 3 too many.

Application

  2. Add the codewords: 0101 + 0111 = 1100. There is no carry-out, and 1100 represents 12 = x + y + 6.

  3. Subtract 0011: 1100 − 0011 = 1001. The code 1001 represents 9 = 6 + 3, which is the Excess-3 encoding of the decimal sum 6.

title: BCD stands for
subject: Digital Electronics
text: BCD stands for
solution:
Concept

Digital circuits operate purely in binary, but humans and displays read decimal digits, so digital systems need a bridge code that lets each individual decimal digit (0–9) be represented by its own small group of bits. The most common such bridge is the 8421 weighted code, universally called BCD.

Application

The acronym names exactly this scheme: “Binary” is the base-2 alphabet the bits are drawn from; “Coded” is the digit-by-digit encoding process; “Decimal” is the base-10 digit that actually gets encoded. So BCD = Binary Coded Decimal. For example, decimal 47 is stored in BCD as 0100 0111 (4 → 0100, 7 → 0111) — two separate 4-bit groups, one per decimal digit — unlike the plain binary form of 47, which is the single pattern 101111.

Cross-check / contrast

Each remaining option swaps out one of the three words for a near-miss term that breaks the standard name:

  • “Binary Coded Digit” replaces the number-system name with the generic word “digit,” which does not identify which base is being represented, so it cannot correctly complete the term.

  • “Bit Coded Decimal” replaces the number-system name with “bit” — a single storage unit, not the name of a number system — so it misnames the first word of the acronym.

  • “Bit Coded Digit” makes both substitutions at once, combining the errors of the two options above.

Binary Coded Decimal is therefore the term BCD stands for.

optionFeedback.html: This is the standard, universally used expansion: the encoding system is “Binary” (base-2), the process is “Coded,” and what gets encoded is each “Decimal” digit (0–9) via its own 4-bit binary pattern — exactly matching how the 8421 weighted code works.

“Binary Coded Digit” sounds plausible because “Digit” is an extremely common, general-purpose word in numbering topics — but this exact phrase is not the accepted, standard expansion of BCD found in digital-electronics and computer-organization references.

“Bit Coded Decimal” sounds plausible because “Bit” is one of the most common words in digital electronics — but this exact phrase is not the accepted, standard expansion of BCD found in digital-electronics and computer-organization references.

“Bit Coded Digit” sounds plausible because both “Bit” and “Digit” are extremely common words in this subject area — but this exact phrase is not the accepted, standard expansion of BCD found in digital-electronics and computer-organization references.
